claim: ATP at millimolar levels has recently been implicated in the solubilization of cellular proteins.
source: Adenosine triphosphate (ATP) at millimolar levels has recently been implicated in the solubilization of cellular proteins.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research in the introduction section.

claim: AMPK and adenylate kinase (ADK) cooperated to maintain cellular ATP levels regardless of glucose levels.
source: We herein demonstrated that AMP-activated protein kinase (AMPK) and adenylate kinase (ADK) cooperated to maintain cellular ATP levels regardless of glucose levels.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript showing ATP levels in various mutants.

claim: ATP levels in ATP-reduced yeast mutants underwent stochastic and transient depletion.
source: Single-cell imaging of ATP-reduced yeast mutants revealed that ATP levels in these mutants underwent stochastic and transient depletion, which promoted the cytotoxic aggregation of endogenous proteins and pathogenic proteins, such as huntingtin and α-synuclein.
evidence: This claim is supported by time-lapse imaging data showing ATP dips in mutant cells.

claim: Transient ATP depletion promoted the cytotoxic aggregation of endogenous proteins and pathogenic proteins, such as huntingtin and α-synuclein.
source: Single-cell imaging of ATP-reduced yeast mutants revealed that ATP levels in these mutants underwent stochastic and transient depletion, which promoted the cytotoxic aggregation of endogenous proteins and pathogenic proteins, such as huntingtin and α-synuclein.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing protein aggregation in ATP-reduced mutants.

claim: Pharmacological elevations in ATP levels in an ATP-reduced mutant prevented the accumulation of α-synuclein aggregates and its cytotoxicity.
source: Moreover, pharmacological elevations in ATP levels in an ATP-reduced mutant prevented the accumulation of α-synuclein aggregates and its cytotoxicity.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the effect of adenine supplementation on α-synuclein aggregation.

claim: Cellular ATP homeostasis ensures proteostasis.
source: The present study demonstrates that cellular ATP homeostasis ensures proteostasis and revealed that suppressing the high volatility of cellular ATP levels prevented cytotoxic protein aggregation, implying that AMPK and ADK are important factors that prevent proteinopathies, such as neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by the experimental findings presented throughout the manuscript.

claim: Suppressing the high volatility of cellular ATP levels prevented cytotoxic protein aggregation.
source: The present study demonstrates that cellular ATP homeostasis ensures proteostasis and revealed that suppressing the high volatility of cellular ATP levels prevented cytotoxic protein aggregation, implying that AMPK and ADK are important factors that prevent proteinopathies, such as neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data showing the relationship between ATP stability and protein aggregation.

claim: AMPK and ADK are important factors that prevent proteinopathies, such as neurodegenerative diseases.
source: The present study demonstrates that cellular ATP homeostasis ensures proteostasis and revealed that suppressing the high volatility of cellular ATP levels prevented cytotoxic protein aggregation, implying that AMPK and ADK are important factors that prevent proteinopathies, such as neurodegenerative diseases.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from the experimental findings and speculation about implications for disease.

claim: ATP has recently been suggested to influence the balance between the soluble and aggregated states of proteins.
source: In addition to its role as energy currency, ATP has recently been suggested to influence the balance between the soluble and aggregated states of proteins, indicating that proteostasis is maintained by energy-dependent chaperones and also by the property of ATP as a hydrotrope to solubilize proteins (Hayes et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2017; Pu et al., 2019; Sridharan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Proteostasis is maintained by energy-dependent chaperones and also by the property of ATP as a hydrotrope to solubilize proteins.
source: In addition to its role as energy currency, ATP has recently been suggested to influence the balance between the soluble and aggregated states of proteins, indicating that proteostasis is maintained by energy-dependent chaperones and also by the property of ATP as a hydrotrope to solubilize proteins (Hayes et al., 2018; Patel et al., 2017; Pu et al., 2019; Sridharan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: ATP levels have been shown to regulate the physicochemical properties of the cytoplasm, such as viscosity, macromolecular crowding, and liquid–liquid phase separation.
source: Furthermore, ATP levels have been shown to regulate the physicochemical properties of the cytoplasm, such as viscosity, macromolecular crowding, and liquid–liquid phase separation (Marini et al., 2020; Persson et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Intracellular ATP levels did not vary within a yeast population grown in the same culture.
source: The findings obtained demonstrated that intracellular ATP levels did not vary within a yeast population grown in the same culture (Takaine et al., 2019), which was in contrast to the large variations observed in intracellular ATP levels within a bacterial cell population (Yaginuma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Large variations were observed in intracellular ATP levels within a bacterial cell population.
source: The findings obtained demonstrated that intracellular ATP levels did not vary within a yeast population grown in the same culture (Takaine et al., 2019), which was in contrast to the large variations observed in intracellular ATP levels within a bacterial cell population (Yaginuma et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Intracellular ATP levels in individual living yeast cells were stably and robustly maintained at approximately 4 mM, irrespective of carbon sources and cell-cycle stages.
source: Moreover, intracellular ATP levels in individual living yeast cells were stably and robustly maintained at approximately 4 mM, irrespective of carbon sources and cell-cycle stages, and temporal fluctuations in intracellular ATP levels were small (Takaine et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: Temporal fluctuations in intracellular ATP levels were small in wild-type yeast cells.
source: Moreover, intracellular ATP levels in individual living yeast cells were stably and robustly maintained at approximately 4 mM, irrespective of carbon sources and cell-cycle stages, and temporal fluctuations in intracellular ATP levels were small (Takaine et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research by the authors.

claim: ATP is stably maintained at a markedly higher level than the Km (Michaelis constant) required for the enzymatic activities of most ATPases.
source: It currently remains unclear why ATP is stably maintained at a markedly higher level than the Km (Michaelis constant) required for the enzymatic activities of most ATPases (Edelman et al., 1987), and the consequences associated with failed ATP homeostasis in living organisms have not yet been elucidated.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AMPK is activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP.
source: AMPK, which is activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP (Xiao et al., 2007), has long been regarded as an important regulator of the whole-body and cellular energy status in eukaryotes (Hardie et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AMPK has long been regarded as an important regulator of the whole-body and cellular energy status in eukaryotes.
source: AMPK, which is activated by AMP and inhibited by ATP (Xiao et al., 2007), has long been regarded as an important regulator of the whole-body and cellular energy status in eukaryotes (Hardie et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AMPK is activated by increases in the AMP:ATP or ADP:ATP ratio.
source: AMPK is activated by increases in the AMP:ATP or ADP:ATP ratio (i.e., low-energy state), and regulates its downstream effectors by phosphorylation to redirect cell metabolism from an anabolic (ATP-consuming) state to catabolic (ATP-producing) state (Herzig and Shaw, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: AMPK regulates its downstream effectors by phosphorylation to redirect cell metabolism from an anabolic (ATP-consuming) state to catabolic (ATP-producing) state.
source: AMPK is activated by increases in the AMP:ATP or ADP:ATP ratio (i.e., low-energy state), and regulates its downstream effectors by phosphorylation to redirect cell metabolism from an anabolic (ATP-consuming) state to catabolic (ATP-producing) state (Herzig and Shaw, 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The yeast Snf1 complex comprises three subunits: the catalytic α subunit (SNF1), scaffolding β subunit (SIP1, SIP2, or GAL83), and regulatory γ subunit (SNF4).
source: Similar to other AMPKs, the yeast Snf1 complex comprises three subunits: the catalytic α subunit (SNF1), scaffolding β subunit (SIP1, SIP2, or GAL83), and regulatory γ subunit (SNF4) (Ghillebert et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The role of the Snf1 complex in adaptation to glucose limitations has been characterized in detail.
source: The role of the Snf1 complex in adaptation to glucose limitations has been characterized in detail (Hedbacker and Carlson, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The Snf1 complex is inactive in the presence of sufficient glucose levels in media.
source: The Snf1 complex is inactive in the presence of sufficient glucose levels in media (Wilson et al., 1996).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Decreases in glucose levels activate the Snf1 complex and phosphorylate the transcriptional repressor Mig1, which then triggers the transcription of numerous glucose-repressed genes.
source: Decreases in glucose levels have been shown to activate the Snf1 complex and phosphorylate the transcriptional repressor Mig1, which then triggers the transcription of numerous glucose-repressed genes (Carlson, 1999).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: The null mutant of ADK (adk1∆) has a reduced cellular ATP level (~70% of the wild type).
source: Adenylate kinase (ADK) is a key enzyme that synthesizes ATP and AMP using two adenosine diphosphate (ADP) molecules as substrates, and the null mutant of ADK (adk1∆) was shown to have a reduced cellular ATP level (~70% of the wild type) (Gauthier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Bas1 is a transcription factor that is required for de novo purine synthesis.
source: Bas1 is a transcription factor that is required for de novo purine synthesis and bas1∆ also has a reduced ATP level (~50% of the wild type) (Gauthier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: bas1∆ has a reduced ATP level (~50% of the wild type).
source: Bas1 is a transcription factor that is required for de novo purine synthesis and bas1∆ also has a reduced ATP level (~50% of the wild type) (Gauthier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.

claim: Cellular ATP levels were significantly lower in SNF1-null mutant (snf1∆) cells than in wild-type cells at various glucose levels.
source: Cellular ATP levels were significantly lower in SNF1-null mutant (snf1∆) cells than in wild-type cells at various glucose levels (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: snf1∆ cells showed significantly reduced ATP levels even under high glucose conditions (2% glucose), at which the Snf1 complex is considered to be inactive.
source: It is important to note that in addition to low glucose conditions (0.05% glucose), at which the Snf1 complex is active, snf1∆ cells showed significantly reduced ATP levels even under high glucose conditions (2% glucose), at which the Snf1 complex is considered to be inactive.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The deletion of each gene encoding the β subunit of AMPK (SIP1, SIP2, or GAL83) reduced cellular ATP levels to a similar extent as the deletion of SNF1.
source: Moreover, the deletion of each gene encoding the β subunit of AMPK (SIP1, SIP2, or GAL83) reduced cellular ATP levels to a similar extent as the deletion of SNF1, suggesting that three subtypes of the Snf1 complex were involved in maintaining ATP concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Three subtypes of the Snf1 complex were involved in maintaining ATP concentrations.
source: Moreover, the deletion of each gene encoding the β subunit of AMPK (SIP1, SIP2, or GAL83) reduced cellular ATP levels to a similar extent as the deletion of SNF1, suggesting that three subtypes of the Snf1 complex were involved in maintaining ATP concentrations (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The deletion of MIG1 had a negligible effect on ATP levels.
source: On the other hand, the deletion of MIG1 had a negligible effect on ATP levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that as yet unknown factors other than Mig1 primarily regulate ATP levels under the control of the Snf1 complex.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: As yet unknown factors other than Mig1 primarily regulate ATP levels under the control of the Snf1 complex.
source: On the other hand, the deletion of MIG1 had a negligible effect on ATP levels (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), suggesting that as yet unknown factors other than Mig1 primarily regulate ATP levels under the control of the Snf1 complex.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: AMPK/SNF1 affect cellular ATP levels even under glucose-rich conditions.
source: Collectively, these results demonstrated for the first time that AMPK/SNF1 affect cellular ATP levels even under glucose-rich conditions.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: adk1∆ cells showed significantly lower QUEEN ratios than wild-type cells on average in the presence of sufficient carbon sources.
source: We confirmed these findings using an ATP imaging method: adk1∆ cells showed significantly lower QUEEN ratios than wild-type cells on average in the presence of sufficient carbon sources (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: snf1∆ adk1∆ cells had significantly lower average ATP levels than single mutant cells.
source: snf1∆ adk1∆ cells had significantly lower average ATP levels than single mutant cells.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: There was a marked variation in ATP levels in the snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆ cell population, as indicated by the large coefficient of variance (CV).
source: We also found not only a general reduction, but also a marked variation in ATP levels in the snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆ cell population, as indicated by the large coefficient of variance (CV) (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Some snf1∆ adk1∆ cells had very low ATP levels.
source: Furthermore, some snf1∆ adk1∆ cells had very low ATP levels (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Adk1 and the Snf1 complex both synergistically contribute to ATP homeostasis.
source: These results suggest that Adk1 and the Snf1 complex both synergistically contribute to ATP homeostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The decreases observed in ATP levels in snf1∆, adk1∆, and snf1∆ adk1∆ cells were confirmed using a biochemical assay of whole cell extract.
source: We confirmed the decreases observed in ATP levels in snf1∆, adk1∆, and snf1∆ adk1∆ cells using a biochemical assay of whole cell extract (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: ADP levels were also reduced in snf1∆, adk1∆, and snf1∆ adk1∆ mutant cells.
source: ADP levels were also reduced in these mutant cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: In adk1∆ cells, the ATP/ADP ratio increased, whereas the sum of ATP and ADP levels decreased.
source: In adk1∆ cells, the ATP/ADP ratio increased, whereas the sum of ATP and ADP levels decreased (Figure 1—figure supplement 3C,D), which is consistent with previous findings (Gauthier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: ATP levels quantified by QUEEN were reduced by ~50% in bas1∆ cells.
source: Consistent with previous biochemical findings (Gauthier et al., 2008), ATP levels quantified by QUEEN were reduced by ~50% in bas1∆ cells (Figure 1D, E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: There was a marked variation in ATP levels in the bas1∆ cell population, as indicated by the large CV.
source: We found not only a general reduction, but also a marked variation in ATP levels in the bas1∆ cell population, as indicated by the large CV (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The addition of extra adenine to media partially restored ATP levels in bas1∆ cells.
source: The decrease observed in ATP levels was due to reduced adenine biosynthesis because the addition of extra adenine to media partially restored ATP levels (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The sufficient production of adenine nucleotides is essential for the stable maintenance of ATP levels.
source: These results suggest that the sufficient production of adenine nucleotides is essential for the stable maintenance of ATP levels.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The role of Bas1 in maintaining ATP levels appeared to be epistatic to that of Snf1.
source: Moreover, the role of Bas1 in maintaining ATP levels appeared to be epistatic to that of Snf1 because bas1∆ snf1∆ double mutant cells showed a similar distribution of ATP levels to bas1∆ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The decrease observed in ATP levels in bas1∆ cells was confirmed using a biochemical assay.
source: We confirmed the decrease observed in ATP levels in bas1∆ cells using a biochemical assay (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: ADP levels and the sum of ATP and ADP levels significantly decreased in bas1∆ cells.
source: ADP levels and the sum of ATP and ADP levels also significantly decreased in bas1∆ cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 3A,D), which is consistent with previous findings (Gauthier et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: The QUEEN ratio underwent a rapid decline followed by recovery in snf1∆ adk1∆ cells.
source: We found that the QUEEN ratio underwent a rapid decline followed by recovery in snf1∆ adk1∆ cells (see 116 and 132 min in Figure 2B, D, and Figure 2—video 1, and 180 and 356 min in Figure 2C, E, and Figure 2—video 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: The sudden decrease in ATP levels (the ATP dip) occurred within a few minutes without any sign and was scarcely observed in wild-type cells.
source: The sudden decrease in ATP levels (hereafter called 'the ATP dip', see Materials and methods for the detailed definition) occurred within a few minutes without any sign and was scarcely observed in wild-type cells (Figure 2A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: 35% of snf1∆ adk1∆ cells exhibited the ATP shift or ATP dip, whereas 99% of wild-type cells showed stable ATP dynamics.
source: In total, 35% of snf1∆ adk1∆ cells exhibited the ATP shift or ATP dip, whereas 99% of wild-type cells showed stable ATP dynamics (Figure 2F).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The ATP dip and shift appeared to be a stochastic event that is intrinsic to cells.
source: The ATP dip and shift appeared to be a stochastic event that is intrinsic to cells; these events occurred independent of the cell-cycle stage or cell size (compare Figure 2D, E).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A correlation was not observed between the duration of the ATP dip and the extent of the decrease in the QUEEN ratio.
source: Moreover, a correlation was not observed between the duration of the ATP dip and the extent of the decrease in the QUEEN ratio (Figure 2—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The marked variations observed in ATP levels in snf1∆ adk1∆ cells were not simply due to a mixed population with different basal ATP levels, but were rather caused by the stochastic ATP dip in individual cells.
source: These results suggest that the marked variations observed in ATP levels in snf1∆ adk1∆ cells were not simply due to a mixed population with different basal ATP levels, but were rather caused by the stochastic ATP dip in individual cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: ATP cycling in bas1Δ cells was slow (~35 min on average) and distinguishable from that in snf1Δ adk1Δcells.
source: Time-lapse imaging of bas1∆ revealed oscillatory cycles in ATP levels (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, and Figure 2—video 3 and Figure 2—video 4): ATP cycling in bas1Δ cells was slow (~35 min on average, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) and distinguishable from that in snf1Δ adk1Δcells; however, the common characteristics of these mutants were that the level of ATP often reached close to 0 mM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: The common characteristics of bas1Δ and snf1Δ adk1Δ mutants were that the level of ATP often reached close to 0 mM.
source: Time-lapse imaging of bas1∆ revealed oscillatory cycles in ATP levels (Figure 2G and Figure 2—figure supplement 3A, and Figure 2—video 3 and Figure 2—video 4): ATP cycling in bas1Δ cells was slow (~35 min on average, Figure 2—figure supplement 3B) and distinguishable from that in snf1Δ adk1Δcells; however, the common characteristics of these mutants were that the level of ATP often reached close to 0 mM.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and videos.

claim: The ATP oscillation cycle was unsynchronized in the population and independent of cell-cycle progression, suggesting a unique metabolic rhythm intrinsic to each cell.
source: The ATP oscillation cycle was unsynchronized in the population and independent of cell-cycle progression, suggesting a unique metabolic rhythm intrinsic to each cell.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: An in silico analysis identified genes involved in 'protein folding/glycosylation' as common negative genetic interactors with adk1∆ and bas1∆.
source: An in silico analysis identified genes involved in 'protein folding/glycosylation' as common negative genetic interactors with adk1∆ and bas1∆ (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genetic interaction data shown in figures.

claim: Negative genetic interactors of ura6 were enriched in the 'protein folding/glycosylation' category.
source: Negative genetic interactors of ura6, a gene encoding uridylate kinase that also exhibits ADK activity, were enriched in the 'protein folding/glycosylation' category (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genetic interaction data shown in figures.

claim: Interactors of snf1 were implicated in 'protein folding/glycosylation'.
source: We also found that interactors of snf1 were implicated in 'protein folding/glycosylation'.
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genetic interaction data.

claim: None of the ATP mutants exhibited apparent genetic interactions with genes in the 'metabolism' category.
source: None of these mutants exhibited apparent genetic interactions with genes in the 'metabolism' category (Figure 3A).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational analysis of genetic interaction data shown in figures.

claim: Although the three mutants regulate ATP with distinct mechanisms, all three have a common cellular function.
source: These results imply that although these three mutants regulate ATP with distinct mechanisms, all three have a common cellular function.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from genetic interaction data.

claim: The adk1 and bas1 mutants both exhibited severe growth defects with a high temperature of 40°C, 1 hr of heat shock at 55°C, or in the presence of 0.5 µg/ml of the glycosylation inhibitor tunicamycin or 2 mM H2O2.
source: However, the adk1 and bas1 mutants both exhibited severe growth defects with a high temperature of 40°C, 1 hr of heat shock at 55°C, or in the presence of 0.5 µg/ml of the glycosylation inhibitor tunicamycin or 2 mM H2O2, an inducer of oxidative stress.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data presented in the manuscript.

claim: The SNF1 deletion increased the stress sensitivity of adk1∆.
source: The SNF1 deletion increased the stress sensitivity of adk1∆ (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: ATP homeostasis mutants are defective in some aspects of proteostasis.
source: This sensitivity to proteotoxic stress suggests that ATP homeostasis mutants are defective in some aspects of proteostasis.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: All four mutants tested contained significantly increased numbers of Hsp104-GFP foci, a marker of protein aggregation.
source: We found that all four mutants tested contained significantly increased numbers of Hsp104-GFP foci, a marker of protein aggregation (Kirkwood et al., 2017; Figure 3C, D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: In contrast to Hsp104-GFP foci, Pab1-GFP, a marker of stress granule (SG) assembly, did not form foci in ATP mutants.
source: In contrast to Hsp104-GFP foci, Pab1-GFP, a marker of stress granule (SG) assembly (Hoyle et al., 2007), did not form foci in ATP mutants, suggesting that protein aggregation and SG assembly are regulated in a distinct manner (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: Protein aggregation and SG assembly are regulated in a distinct manner.
source: In contrast to Hsp104-GFP foci, Pab1-GFP, a marker of stress granule (SG) assembly (Hoyle et al., 2007), did not form foci in ATP mutants, suggesting that protein aggregation and SG assembly are regulated in a distinct manner (Figure 3D).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Within 15 min of the 2DG treatment, more than 20% of cells contained Hsp104-GFP foci indicative of protein aggregation.
source: Within 15 min of the 2DG treatment, more than 20% of cells contained Hsp104-GFP foci indicative of protein aggregation (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: Protein aggregations were retained for hours after refeeding of glucose.
source: These protein aggregations were retained for hours after refeeding of glucose (Figure 4A, B), suggesting that the dissolution kinetics of Hsp104-GFP were significantly slow.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The dissolution kinetics of Hsp104-GFP were significantly slow.
source: These protein aggregations were retained for hours after refeeding of glucose (Figure 4A, B), suggesting that the dissolution kinetics of Hsp104-GFP were significantly slow.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: ATP depletion by the 2DG treatment triggered Ubc9-ts protein aggregation.
source: To further confirm whether a high level of ATP is required for protein solubility, we also tested the Ubc9-ts protein, a model protein that is prone to aggregation (Kaganovich et al., 2008), and found that ATP depletion by the 2DG treatment triggered Ubc9-ts protein aggregation (Figure 4C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: Not only Hsp104-GFP-positive intrinsic proteins, but also extrinsic model proteins aggregate after ATP depletion.
source: Therefore, not only Hsp104-GFP-positive intrinsic proteins, but also extrinsic model proteins aggregate after ATP depletion.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: ATP depletion after the 2DG treatment did not instantly trigger the formation of SG.
source: In contrast to the formation of Hsp104-GFP foci, ATP depletion after the 2DG treatment did not instantly trigger the formation of SG (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: SG formation requires ATP.
source: Consistent with recent findings (Jain et al., 2016), the present results suggest that SG formation requires ATP.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data and citation to prior research.

claim: Hsp104-GFP foci and SG did not colocalize, indicating that these structures are derived from distinct mechanisms.
source: We also noted that Hsp104-GFP foci and SG did not colocalize, indicating that these structures are derived from distinct mechanisms (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The artificial depletion of ATP may trigger abnormal protein aggregation in living yeast cells.
source: Therefore, the artificial depletion of ATP may trigger abnormal protein aggregation in living yeast cells.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The expression of Syn-GFP exhibited negligible toxicity against wild-type yeast when expressed under the inducible GAL1 promotor.
source: As reported previously, the expression of Syn-GFP exhibited negligible toxicity against wild-type yeast when expressed under the inducible GAL1 promotor (Figure 5A; Outeiro and Lindquist, 2003; Sharma et al., 2006; Wijayanti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to prior research.

claim: snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆, and bas1∆ were hypersensitive to the expression of Syn-GFP.
source: However, snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆, and bas1∆ were hypersensitive to the expression of Syn-GFP (Figure 5A).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: rpn4Δ was very sensitive to Syn-GFP.
source: We also found that rpn4Δ, which encodes a key transcription factor for proteasomal subunits (Xie and Varshavsky, 2001), was very sensitive to Syn-GFP (Figure 5A), which is consistent with the concept that Syn-GFP is degraded in the ubiquitin–proteasomal pathway in yeast (Tofaris et al., 2011; Wijayanti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citations to prior research.

claim: Syn-GFP is degraded in the ubiquitin–proteasomal pathway in yeast.
source: We also found that rpn4Δ, which encodes a key transcription factor for proteasomal subunits (Xie and Varshavsky, 2001), was very sensitive to Syn-GFP (Figure 5A), which is consistent with the concept that Syn-GFP is degraded in the ubiquitin–proteasomal pathway in yeast (Tofaris et al., 2011; Wijayanti et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Syn-GFP expressed in yeast mainly localized to the plasma membrane.
source: Consistent with previous findings (Willingham et al., 2003), Syn-GFP expressed in yeast mainly localized to the plasma membrane (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and citation to prior research.

claim: Syn-GFP localized to punctate structures, most likely corresponding to protein aggregation.
source: In addition to the plasma membrane, we found that Syn-GFP localized to punctate structures, most likely corresponding to protein aggregation (Figure 5B, C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures and inference.

claim: The accumulation of Syn-GFP puncta was not simply due to defective degradation.
source: Punctate structures were not as obvious in rpn4∆ cells defective in proteasomes, suggesting that the accumulation of Syn-GFP puncta was not simply due to defective degradation.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The addition of adenine-reduced Syn-GFP toxicity and aggregation in bas1Δ, but not adk1Δ cells.
source: Consistent with our hypothesis, the addition of adenine-reduced Syn-GFP toxicity and aggregation in bas1Δ, but not adk1Δ cells (Figure 5D).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: A high level of ATP prevented Syn-GFP aggregation and toxicity.
source: Thus, a high level of ATP prevented Syn-GFP aggregation and toxicity.
evidence: This claim is based on inference from experimental data.

claim: The ATP homeostasis mutants snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆, and bas1∆ were very sensitive to Htt103Q expression.
source: Consistent with the concept that a high level of ATP prevents protein aggregation, the ATP homeostasis mutants snf1∆, adk1∆, snf1∆ adk1∆, and bas1∆ were very sensitive to Htt103Q expression (Figure 5—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in figures.

claim: The deletion of RPN4 resulted in synthetic growth defects with adk1∆, snf1∆, bas1∆ at a high temperature of 38°C and in the presence of H2O2.

claim: The Snf1 complex is required for the stable maintenance of cellular ATP levels (ATP homeostasis) in collaboration with Adk1.
source: In the present study, we demonstrated for the first time that the Snf1 complex, budding yeast AMPK, is required for the stable maintenance of cellular ATP levels (ATP homeostasis) in collaboration with Adk1 (Figure 8A).

claim: The function of the Snf1 complex in ATP homeostasis is independent of glucose levels in the medium and Mig1.

claim: The activity of the Snf1 kinase complex may be sharply tuned depending on the intracellular levels of adenine nucleotides or other metabolites indicative of cellular energy to prevent a rapid ATP dip.

claim: The deletion of SNF1 decreased glycolytic flux in cells cultured in 1% glucose.

claim: A large pool size of adenine nucleotides is a prerequisite for ATP homeostasis.

claim: At levels lower than 0.5 mM, ATP mainly serves as a substrate for enzymes, such as protein kinases and heat shock protein chaperones.

At levels lower than 0.5 mM, ATP mainly serves as a substrate for enzymes, such as protein kinases and heat shock protein chaperones, whereas at levels higher than 2 mM, ATP may exert solubilizing effects on disordered proteins (Sridharan et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to prior research.
